verses.text: This happened in the days of Ahasuerus, the Ahasuerus who ruled 127 provinces from India all the way to Ethiopia.
At the time, King Ahasuerus ruled from his royal throne in the palace at Susa.
In his third year as king, he threw a feast for all his officials and servants. The army of Persia and Media was there, along with the nobles and provincial leaders.
For a full 180 days, he showed off the wealth of his glorious kingdom and the splendor of his royal majesty.
When those days were over, the king threw a seven-day feast in the courtyard of his palace garden. Everyone at the palace in Susa was invited, from the most important to the least.
White and blue hangings were tied with fine linen and purple cords to silver rings and marble pillars. Gold and silver couches stood on a floor of red, white, yellow, and black marble.
Drinks came in gold cups of all kinds. There was plenty of royal wine, thanks to the king’s generosity.
Under the rules, no one had to drink. The king had told all his household officials to let each guest decide for himself.
Queen Vashti also threw a feast for the women in King Ahasuerus’s royal house.
On the seventh day, when the wine had put the king in high spirits, he gave an order to Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcass, the seven eunuchs who served him in person.
He told them to bring Queen Vashti before him wearing her royal crown. She was beautiful, and he wanted to show off her beauty to the people and the officials.
But Queen Vashti refused to come when the eunuchs brought the king’s order. The king was furious. His anger burned inside him.
The king turned to the wise men who understood the times. It was his custom to consult those who knew the law and how to judge a case.

The men closest to him were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven leaders of Persia and Media who had access to the king and held the highest places in the kingdom.
The king asked, “Under the law, what should we do about Queen Vashti? She didn’t obey the order King Ahasuerus sent through the eunuchs.”
Memucan answered in front of the king and his officials, “Queen Vashti has wronged more than the king. She’s wronged all the officials and everyone in every province of King Ahasuerus.

Women everywhere will hear what the queen did. When the word gets around that ‘King Ahasuerus ordered Queen Vashti to be brought before him, but she wouldn’t come,’ they’ll look down on their husbands.
Today the noblewomen of Persia and Media who’ve heard what the queen did will tell it to all the king’s officials. It’ll lead to plenty of contempt and anger.

“If it pleases the king, issue a royal order and write it into the laws of Persia and Media so it can’t be changed. Let Vashti never come before King Ahasuerus again, and let the king give her royal position to someone better than she is.
When the king’s order goes out across his whole kingdom, vast as it is, wives everywhere will honor their husbands, whoever they are.”
The king and his officials liked the advice, so the king did what Memucan suggested.
He sent letters to every province, using each province’s script and each people’s language. The order said every man was to rule his own household and speak the language of his own people.
Later, when King Ahasuerus had cooled down, he thought about Vashti, what she’d done, and the order that had been issued against her.
Then the servants who attended the king said, “Let a search be made for beautiful young virgins for the king.

Appoint officers in every province to gather all the beautiful young virgins at the fortress in Susa. Bring them to the women’s quarters under the care of Hegai, the king’s eunuch in charge of the women. Give them beauty treatments.
Then make the young woman who pleases the king queen in Vashti’s place.” The king liked the idea and went ahead with it.
There was a Jewish man in the fortress at Susa named Mordecai. He was a Benjaminite, the son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish.
He’d been taken from Jerusalem with the exiles who went into captivity with King Jeconiah of Judah when King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon took him away.

Mordecai raised Hadassah, also known as Esther, his uncle’s daughter. She had no father or mother. Esther was lovely and beautiful, and when her parents died, Mordecai took her in as his own daughter.

When word of the king’s order got out, many young women were brought to the fortress at Susa and put in Hegai’s care. Esther was taken to the king’s house and put in the care of Hegai, who was in charge of the women.

Esther made a good impression on Hegai, and he treated her kindly. He quickly gave her beauty treatments and her share of food, along with seven specially chosen young women from the king’s household. He moved Esther and her attendants to the best part of the women’s quarters.
Esther hadn’t told anyone about her people or her family because Mordecai had told her to keep it to herself.
Every day Mordecai walked in front of the courtyard of the women’s quarters to find out how Esther was doing and what would happen to her.
Each young woman went in to King Ahasuerus when her turn came, after twelve months of preparation. The routine was six months with myrrh oil and six months with fragrances and beauty treatments.
When a young woman went to the king, she could take whatever she asked for from the women’s quarters to the king’s house.

She went in the evening, and the next day she returned to a second set of women’s quarters under Shaashgaz, the king’s eunuch in charge of the concubines. She didn’t go back to the king unless he was pleased with her and called for her by name.

When Esther’s turn came, she asked for only what Hegai, the king’s eunuch in charge of the women, recommended. Esther was the daughter of Abihail, Mordecai’s uncle, and Mordecai had taken her in as his daughter. Everyone who saw her took a liking to her.
Esther was taken to King Ahasuerus at his royal house in Tebeth, the tenth month of his seventh year as king.

The king loved Esther more than any of the other women. She won more favor and kindness from him than any of the other virgins. So he put the royal crown on her head and made her queen in Vashti’s place.
Then the king threw a big feast for all his officials and servants in Esther’s honor. He declared a holiday in the provinces and handed out gifts with royal generosity.
When the virgins were gathered a second time, Mordecai was sitting at the king’s gate.
Esther still hadn’t told anyone about her family or her people, just as Mordecai had told her. She obeyed him the way she had when he was raising her.
Around that time, while Mordecai was sitting at the king’s gate, two of the king’s eunuchs, Bigthan and Teresh, who guarded the doors, got angry and plotted to lay hands on King Ahasuerus.
Mordecai found out about the plot and told Queen Esther. She passed it on to the king and gave Mordecai the credit.
They investigated and found the report was true. Both men were hanged on a gallows, and it was written in the royal record book in the king’s presence.
After all this, King Ahasuerus promoted Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite. He raised him to a seat above all the other officials who served with him.
All the king’s servants at the royal gate bowed down and paid Haman respect, because the king had ordered it. But Mordecai wouldn’t bow down or pay him homage.
The king’s servants at the gate asked Mordecai, “Why are you disobeying the king’s order?”
They asked him day after day, and he wouldn’t listen. So they told Haman to see whether Mordecai’s reason would hold up. Mordecai had told them he was Jewish.
When Haman saw that Mordecai wouldn’t bow down or pay him homage, he was furious.
But to Haman, going after Mordecai alone wasn’t enough. They’d told him who Mordecai’s people were, so Haman set out to destroy Mordecai’s people, all the Jews throughout Ahasuerus’s kingdom.
In Nisan, the first month of King Ahasuerus’s twelfth year, they cast Pur, which means the lot, in front of Haman for the days and months. The lot fell on Adar, the twelfth month.

Haman told King Ahasuerus, “There’s a certain people scattered among the people of every province in your kingdom. Their laws are different from everybody else’s, and they don’t keep the king’s laws. It’s no good for the king to let them stay.

If it pleases the king, put it in writing that they’re to be destroyed. I’ll pay ten thousand talents of silver to the officials who handle the king’s business so they can put it into the royal treasuries.”
The king took the ring off his hand and gave it to Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews.
The king told Haman, “The silver is yours, and so are the people. Do with them what you think best.”

On the thirteenth day of the first month, the king’s scribes were called in. They wrote down everything Haman ordered and addressed it to the king’s local governors, the governors of every province, and the leaders of every people. Each province got it in its own script, and each people in its own language. It was written in King Ahasuerus’s name and sealed with his ring.

Couriers carried the letters to every province. The order was to destroy, kill, and wipe out all Jews, young and old, little children and women, on a single day, the thirteenth of Adar, the twelfth month, and to plunder their property.
A copy of the letter was to go out as an official order in every province and be made public to all the peoples so they’d be ready for that day.
At the king’s command, the couriers left in a hurry, and the decree went out in the fortress at Susa. The king and Haman sat down for a drink, while the city of Susa was bewildered.
When Mordecai found out everything that had happened, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth and ashes, and went into the middle of the city, crying out loud and bitterly.
He went as far as the king’s gate, because nobody dressed in sackcloth was allowed inside.
In every province the king’s order reached, the Jews went into deep mourning. They fasted, cried, and wailed, and many lay in sackcloth and ashes.
Esther’s attendants and eunuchs came and told her, and the queen was deeply upset. She sent Mordecai clothes to wear in place of the sackcloth, but he wouldn’t take them.
Then Esther called Hathach, one of the king’s eunuchs appointed to attend her. She told him to go to Mordecai and find out what was happening and why.
Hathach went out to Mordecai in the city square in front of the king’s gate.
Mordecai told him everything that had happened to him, including the exact amount Haman had promised to pay into the king’s treasuries to have the Jews destroyed.
He also gave him a copy of the decree issued in Susa ordering their destruction. He told Hathach to show it to Esther, explain it to her, and urge her to go to the king and plead for her people.
Hathach came back and told Esther what Mordecai had said.
Then Esther gave Hathach a message to take to Mordecai:

“Everyone who serves the king and everyone in his provinces knows the rule. If anyone, man or woman, goes into the inner court to see the king without being called, they’re put to death. The only exception is if the king holds out the gold scepter and lets them live. I haven’t been called to see the king in thirty days.”
They passed Esther’s words on to Mordecai.
Mordecai sent back this answer: “Don’t think you’re any more likely to escape than the rest of the Jews just because you live in the king’s house.
If you stay quiet now, relief and rescue will come to the Jews from somewhere else, but you and your father’s family will perish. Who knows? Maybe you became queen for a time like this.”
Then Esther sent Mordecai this answer:

“Go gather all the Jews in Susa and fast for me. Don’t eat or drink for three days, night or day. My attendants and I will fast too. Then I’ll go to the king, even though it’s against the law. If I die, I die.”
So Mordecai went and did everything Esther had told him to do.
On the third day, Esther put on her royal clothes and stood in the palace’s inner court, beside the king’s house. The king sat on his throne inside, by the entrance.
When the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, he looked on her with favor and held out the gold scepter in his hand. Esther stepped forward and touched its tip.
The king asked her, “What is it, Queen Esther? What are you asking for? I’ll give it to you, even if it’s half the kingdom.”
Esther said, “If it pleases the king, I’d like the king and Haman to come today to the banquet I’ve prepared for him.”
The king said, “Bring Haman right away so we can do what Esther asked.” So the king and Haman went to the banquet Esther had prepared.
As they drank wine at the banquet, the king asked Esther, “What are you asking for? I’ll grant it. What do you want? Even if it’s half the kingdom, I’ll do it.”
Esther answered, “Here’s what I’m asking for.
If I’ve found favor with the king, and if he’s willing to grant what I ask, let the king and Haman come to the banquet I’ll prepare for them. Tomorrow I’ll answer the king as he’s asked.”
Haman left that day in high spirits. But then he saw Mordecai at the king’s gate. Mordecai didn’t get up or even move for him, and Haman was furious with him.
Haman held himself back and went home. Once there, he sent for his friends and for his wife Zeresh.
He told them about his impressive wealth, how many children he had, and all the ways the king had promoted him above the other officials and servants.
Haman added, “Queen Esther didn’t invite anybody but me to join the king at the banquet she prepared. And she’s invited me to come back with the king tomorrow too.
But none of that does me any good as long as I keep seeing Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king’s gate.”

Then his wife Zeresh and all his friends said, “Have a gallows fifty cubits high made. In the morning, ask the king to have Mordecai hanged on it. Then go enjoy the banquet with the king.” Haman liked the idea and had the gallows made.
That night the king couldn’t sleep. He ordered someone to bring the book of royal records, and they read it to him.
They found the account of how Mordecai had reported Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king’s eunuchs who guarded the doors. They’d tried to lay hands on King Ahasuerus.
The king asked, “How did we honor Mordecai for that? What distinction did he receive?” The servants attending him said, “Nothing’s been done for him.”
The king asked, “Who’s in the court?” Haman had just come into the outer court of the palace to ask the king to hang Mordecai on the gallows he’d made for him.
The king’s servants told him, “Haman is standing in the court.” The king said, “Let him in.”
Haman came in, and the king asked him, “What should be done for the man the king is delighted to honor?” Haman thought, “Who would the king want to honor more than me?”
So Haman told the king, “For the man the king is delighted to honor,
bring out a robe the king himself has worn and a horse the king himself rides, with a royal crown on the horse’s head.

Hand the robe and horse over to one of the king’s highest-ranking officials. Have him dress the man the king wants to honor, lead him on horseback through the city square, and call out ahead of him, ‘This is what’s done for the man the king is delighted to honor!’”
Then the king told Haman, “Quick, take the robe and horse, just as you said, and do all this for Mordecai the Jew, the man who sits at the king’s gate. Don’t leave out a thing you mentioned.”
So Haman took the robe and horse, dressed Mordecai, and led him on horseback through the city square. He called out ahead of him, “This is what’s done for the man the king is delighted to honor!”
Mordecai went back to the king’s gate, but Haman rushed home in grief with his head covered.

Haman told his wife Zeresh and all his friends everything that had happened. His advisers and his wife Zeresh told him, “If Mordecai, the man you’ve already started to fall before, is of Jewish descent, you won’t beat him. You’ll surely fall before him.”
While they were still talking, the king’s eunuchs arrived and hurried Haman off to the banquet Esther had prepared.
The king and Haman came to feast with Queen Esther.
On the second day, as they drank wine at the banquet, the king asked Esther again, “What are you asking for, Queen Esther? I’ll grant it. What do you want? Even if it’s half the kingdom, I’ll do it.”
Queen Esther answered, “If I’ve found favor with you, O king, and if it pleases you, here’s what I ask: spare my life and spare my people.

My people and I have been sold to be destroyed, killed, and wiped out. If we’d only been sold as slaves, men and women alike, I would’ve kept quiet, even though the enemy couldn’t make up for what the king would lose.”
King Ahasuerus asked Queen Esther, “Who would dare do a thing like that? Where is he?”
Esther said, “The enemy, the one against us, is this wicked Haman!” Haman was terrified in front of the king and queen.
The king got up from the wine banquet in a rage and went out to the palace garden. Haman stood up to beg Queen Esther for his life. He could see the king had decided to bring disaster on him.

When the king came back from the palace garden to the banquet room, Haman had fallen across the couch where Esther was. The king said, “Is he going to assault the queen right in front of me, in my own house?” The words were barely out of the king’s mouth when they covered Haman’s face.

Harbonah, one of the eunuchs attending the king, said, “Look, there’s a gallows fifty cubits high standing at Haman’s house. He made it for Mordecai, the man who spoke up for the king’s good.” The king said, “Hang him on it!”
So they hanged Haman on the gallows he’d made for Mordecai. Then the king’s anger cooled.
That day King Ahasuerus gave Queen Esther the estate of Haman, the enemy of the Jews. Mordecai came before the king because Esther had told him how they were related.
The king took off the ring he’d taken back from Haman and gave it to Mordecai. Esther put Mordecai in charge of Haman’s estate.
Esther spoke to the king again. She fell at his feet and begged him through tears to undo the harm Haman the Agagite had set in motion and stop the plot he’d made against the Jews.
The king held out the gold scepter to Esther. She got up and stood before him.

She said, “If it pleases the king, if I’ve found favor with him, if this seems right to him, and if he’s pleased with me, let an order be written to reverse the letters Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite devised to destroy the Jews in every province of the kingdom.
How could I bear to see that disaster come on my people? How could I bear to watch my own family be destroyed?”
King Ahasuerus told Queen Esther and Mordecai the Jew, “Look, I’ve given Esther Haman’s estate, and they’ve hanged him on the gallows because he raised his hand against the Jews.
Now write to the Jews whatever you think best in the king’s name, and seal it with the king’s ring. Nobody can reverse a document written in the king’s name and sealed with his ring.”

The king’s scribes were called in on the twenty-third day of Sivan, the third month. They wrote down everything Mordecai ordered for the Jews, the local governors, and the governors and leaders of the 127 provinces from India to Ethiopia. They wrote in each province’s own script and each people’s own language, including the Jews’ own script and language.
Mordecai wrote in King Ahasuerus’s name and sealed the letters with the king’s ring. He sent them by mounted couriers riding royal horses bred from swift steeds.

The letters gave the Jews in every city permission to gather and defend their lives. They could destroy, kill, and wipe out any force from any people or province that attacked them, their children, or their women, and plunder the attackers’ property.
This was to happen on a single day in all King Ahasuerus’s provinces, the thirteenth day of Adar, the twelfth month.
A copy of the letter was to go out as an official order in every province and be made public to all the peoples, so the Jews could be ready that day to take vengeance on their enemies.
The couriers on the royal horses set out in a hurry, urged on by the king’s command. The decree went out in the fortress at Susa.
Mordecai left the king’s presence in blue and white royal clothes, wearing a large gold crown and a robe of fine linen and purple. The city of Susa shouted and celebrated.
For the Jews there was light, gladness, joy, and honor.

In every province and every city the king’s decree reached, the Jews were glad and joyful. They held feasts and celebrated a holiday. Many of the peoples of the land became Jews because fear of the Jews had come over them.

On the thirteenth day of Adar, the twelfth month, the king’s orders were about to take effect. The enemies of the Jews had hoped to overpower them that day, but it went the other way: the Jews overcame those who hated them.
The Jews gathered in their cities across all King Ahasuerus’s provinces to strike those who meant to harm them. No one could stand against them because fear of them had spread among all the people.
The provincial leaders, local governors, governors, and officials who handled the king’s business all helped the Jews because they were afraid of Mordecai.
Mordecai held a high position in the king’s house. Word about him spread throughout the provinces as he grew more and more influential.
The Jews struck down all their enemies with the sword, killing and destroying them. They did as they wished to those who hated them.
In the fortress at Susa, the Jews killed and destroyed five hundred men.
They killed Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha,
Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha,
Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai, and Vaizatha.
These were the ten sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews. But the Jews took none of the plunder.
That day the count of those killed in the fortress at Susa was brought to the king.

The king said to Queen Esther, “The Jews have killed and destroyed five hundred men in the fortress at Susa, including Haman’s ten sons. What must they have done in the other provinces! Now what are you asking for? I’ll grant it. What else do you want? It’ll be done.”
Esther answered, “If it pleases the king, let the Jews in Susa act under today’s decree tomorrow too, and let Haman’s ten sons be hanged on the gallows.”
The king ordered it done. The decree went out in Susa, and Haman’s ten sons were hanged.
The Jews in Susa gathered again on the fourteenth day of Adar and killed three hundred men in Susa. But they took none of the plunder.

The other Jews in the king’s provinces gathered to defend their lives. They gained relief from their enemies and killed seventy-five thousand of those who hated them. But they took none of the plunder.
They did this on the thirteenth day of Adar. On the fourteenth they rested and made it a day of feasting and celebration.
In Susa, though, the Jews gathered on the thirteenth and the fourteenth. They rested on the fifteenth and made it a day of feasting and celebration.
That’s why Jews in villages and towns without walls celebrate the fourteenth of Adar as a holiday. They feast, celebrate, and send each other gifts of food.
Mordecai wrote these things down and sent letters to Jews near and far in all King Ahasuerus’s provinces.
He told them to observe the fourteenth and fifteenth days of Adar every year.

Those were the days when the Jews got relief from their enemies, in the month when sorrow turned to joy and mourning turned into a holiday. They were to feast and celebrate, send food to one another, and give gifts to people in need.
The Jews agreed to keep up the custom they’d started, just as Mordecai had written to them.
Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted to destroy them. He’d cast Pur, meaning the lot, to wipe them out.
But when the king found out, he issued written orders that Haman’s wicked plot against the Jews should come back on his own head and that he and his sons should be hanged on the gallows.
That’s why they called those days Purim, from the word Pur. Because of everything in that letter, what they’d seen, and what had happened to them,
the Jews made it a lasting obligation for themselves, their descendants, and everyone who joined them to keep those two days each year at the appointed time, just as it was written.
Every generation, family, province, and city was to remember and observe these days. The days of Purim were never to lapse among the Jews, and their descendants were never to forget them.
Then Queen Esther daughter of Abihail and Mordecai the Jew wrote with full authority to confirm this second letter about Purim.
Mordecai sent letters with words of peace and truth to all the Jews in the 127 provinces of Ahasuerus’s kingdom.

The letters confirmed that Purim was to be kept at the appointed times, as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther had directed and as the Jews had committed themselves and their descendants to the practices of fasting and mourning.
Esther’s order confirmed these observances of Purim, and it was written in the book.
King Ahasuerus imposed a tax on the land and the islands of the sea.
Aren’t all the acts that showed his power and might, along with the full account of how the king raised Mordecai to greatness, written in the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia?
Mordecai the Jew ranked second to King Ahasuerus. He was highly respected among the Jews and welcomed by many of his own people. He worked for their good and spoke peace to all his descendants.
